title: Why the cross?
hook: Christians explain it in several ways: ransom, sacrifice, love's example, victory over death

segments.voice: Yesterday, fully God, fully human: four withouts, and a mystery held rather than solved. Your line was both at once. Who did you let be both? Day three hundred two.

Here's a question a child might ask in church, and a very good one. If God can do anything, why did Jesus have to die? Why that way, on a Roman cross, in pain and shame? Couldn't God just forgive? Grown-ups have asked it ever since, and the answer may be unexpected: the creeds shared across the churches never settled on one single explanation. The creeds say he was crucified for us, and they stop there. They say that it matters. They don't fully say how. So Christians over the centuries have reached for pictures, the way you might describe a sunrise with several different words, each catching something true. Today's word is the name for what the cross does, and we'll look at four of those pictures.
screen: `WHY DID HE HAVE TO DIE?` → `NO SINGLE OFFICIAL ANSWER.` → `SEVERAL PICTURES, EACH TRUE.`

segments.voice: Atonement is an English word built from two small ones, at and one. At-one-ment. Being made at one. The King James Bible uses it in Romans: "by whom we have now received the atonement." So the question is: how does the cross make people at one with God? Picture one: a ransom. Jesus said the Son of man came "to give his life a ransom for many." Humanity is held captive, by sin and death, and Jesus pays the price to set people free. Some early Christian writers made a great deal of this picture. Picture two: a sacrifice. Drawing on the temple and the letter to the Hebrews, Christians see Jesus as the offering that takes away sin. In the Middle Ages, Anselm of Canterbury described it as Christ paying the debt of honor humanity owed God. Reformers such as Calvin, and Protestants who follow them, stress that Christ took the penalty for sin in our place. Picture three: love's example. A teacher named Abelard said the cross shows us a love so great it melts our hearts and changes us. "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Picture four: victory. Christ goes into death and breaks it open from the inside, defeating everything that holds people captive. It rings through Orthodox Easter hymns, the song of Easter morning. Different churches lean toward different pictures, and often hold several at once. What runs under all of them is one line from the first letter of John: "Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins." Love, going all the way.
screen: `AT-ONE-MENT.` · `A RANSOM, AND A SACRIFICE.` · `LOVE'S EXAMPLE, AND A VICTORY.` · `MANY PICTURES, ONE LOVE.` · then, large: `HEREIN IS LOVE, NOT THAT WE LOVED GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick the picture that speaks to you. Settle, and breathe. Let the four pass through your mind, slowly. A ransom: someone paying to set a captive free. A sacrifice: someone taking what should have fallen on another. Love's example: a love so big it changes you. A victory: a door broken open from the inside. Notice which one stirs something in you today. Stay with that one. If you pray, you can give thanks for what it shows you. If you don't, just stay with the picture a little longer. The bell holds the time.
Atonement. At-one-ment: being made at one with God. The name for what Christians believe the cross does.
Your line: love went all the way. Today, notice where love costs you something, and go one step further than you would have. Day three hundred two.

howItsDone: Christians remember the cross most of all on Good Friday, and many churches display a cross or crucifix, sing hymns about Christ's death, and remember it at every communion.

fork.setup: a child asks: if God can do anything, why did Jesus have to die? you're a theologian. what do the shared creeds let you say?
options: there's one official explanation, and here it is.
Christians use several pictures, each catching something true.
fork.reveal: the shared creeds never pinned down one theory. ransom, sacrifice, example and victory each catch part of it, under one love.

original.note: Greek: a ransom, the price paid to free a captive. Jesus's word in Mark 10:45.

trapdoor: what you thought: atonement means paying for a mistake.
what it means: being made at one with God. Christians describe how the cross does it in several ways.
what a scholar hears: an English coinage, at-one-ment, and a doctrine no ecumenical council ever pinned to a single theory.

notes: Atonement: the English word 'atonement' (at-one-ment) appears c. 1500s and was popularized by Tyndale's Bible. Script says 'Bible translators in the 1500s'. Confirm.

Four models (ransom, satisfaction/penal substitution, moral influence, Christus Victor) summarized without ranking. Confirm the summaries, especially penal substitution ('took the penalty for sin in our place').
The claim that no ecumenical council defined a single atonement theory is standard; confirm.
Orthodox affinity for the victory picture: common characterization; confirm.
Hook says 'the church has never settled on one single answer' — some traditions have confessional positions (e.g. Reformed confessions on penal substitution). Script says the creeds don't say how.
